# Expression analysis {#sec-expression}

::: {.callout-note title="From the exam description"}
Expression analysis of genes and proteins: methods, algorithms, statistics.
:::

## Introduction

Measuring which genes are expressed, and how much, links the genome to
the phenotype. The first genome-wide methods were DNA microarrays. They
measure the hybridisation of labelled cDNA to probes synthesised on a
chip [@fodor1991] or spotted on glass [@schena1995]. Microarrays
introduced most of the analysis ideas still in use. These include
normalisation between samples, clustering of genes with similar profiles
[@eisen1998], comparisons across tissues [@su2004], and the need to deal
with thousands of statistical tests at once [@quackenbush2001].

RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) has largely replaced microarrays
[@mortazavi2008; @wang2009]. It counts reads from transcripts, so it is
not limited to predefined probes. It covers a larger dynamic range and
can detect new transcripts, isoforms and allele-specific expression. A
typical analysis has several steps [@conesa2016]:

1. Quality control.
2. Alignment to the genome with a splice-aware aligner [@dobin2013], or
   fast "pseudo-alignment" directly to the transcriptome
   [@bray2016; @patro2017].
3. Counting reads per gene or transcript, possibly after transcript
   assembly [@trapnell2010].
4. Normalisation for sequencing depth and composition.
5. Statistical testing for differential expression.

Counts are overdispersed compared with a Poisson distribution, so tools
such as edgeR and DESeq2 model them with the negative binomial
distribution. They borrow information across genes to estimate the
dispersion reliably from only a few replicates
[@robinson2010; @love2014; @oshlack2010]. Lists of differentially
expressed genes are then interpreted with gene-set enrichment methods
[@subramanian2005].

Single-cell RNA-seq measures expression in individual cells. It has
revealed new cell types and developmental trajectories. Its data are
sparse and noisy, and they need dedicated methods for normalisation,
dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP), clustering and annotation
[@luecken2019; @heumos2023]. Spatial transcriptomics also keeps the
position of each measurement in the tissue [@stark2019].

All expression studies share one statistical problem: testing 20,000
genes at a 5% significance level will give about 1,000 false positives
even if nothing changes. Controlling the family-wise error rate
(Bonferroni) is very conservative. The false discovery rate, the expected
proportion of false positives among the reported findings, is usually
the more useful quantity [@benjamini1995; @storey2003; @efron2002].
Exploratory tools such as principal component analysis [@lever2017] are
essential for detecting batch effects and outliers before any testing is
done. Protein-level expression is covered in @sec-proteomics.

## Key concepts

- Microarrays: principle, normalisation, limitations
- RNA-seq workflow: library preparation, spliced alignment (STAR) vs. pseudo-alignment (kallisto, Salmon), transcript assembly
- Normalisation: library size, RPKM/FPKM/TPM, TMM, size factors
- Differential expression: count models (negative binomial), dispersion estimation, DESeq2, edgeR
- Multiple testing: Bonferroni/FWER, false discovery rate (Benjamini–Hochberg), q-values, empirical Bayes
- Clustering (hierarchical, k-means) and dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP)
- Gene set enrichment analysis
- Single-cell RNA-seq: sparsity, normalisation, clustering, cell-type annotation; spatial transcriptomics
- Protein-level expression (see @sec-proteomics); the Human Protein Atlas

## Key papers

::: {.callout-tip}
★ = mandatory in earlier reading lists.
:::

### Reviews — start here

- ★ @wang2009 — RNA-seq: a revolutionary tool for transcriptomics.
- @conesa2016 — a survey of best practices for RNA-seq data analysis.
- @stark2019 — RNA sequencing: the teenage years.
- @heumos2023 — best practices for single-cell analysis across modalities.
- @quackenbush2001 — computational analysis of microarray data.

### Microarrays

- @fodor1991 — light-directed parallel synthesis (the basis of Affymetrix arrays).
- @schena1995 — quantitative monitoring of expression with cDNA microarrays.
- @eisen1998 — cluster analysis and display of genome-wide expression.
- @su2004 — a gene atlas of mouse and human transcriptomes.

### RNA-seq methods

- @mortazavi2008 — mapping and quantifying mammalian transcriptomes by RNA-seq.
- @trapnell2010 — Cufflinks: transcript assembly and quantification.
- @oshlack2010 — from RNA-seq reads to differential expression.
- @robinson2010 — edgeR.
- @love2014 — DESeq2.
- @dobin2013 — STAR spliced aligner.
- @bray2016 — kallisto: near-optimal probabilistic quantification.
- @patro2017 — Salmon.
- @subramanian2005 — gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA).
- @luecken2019 — current best practices in single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

### Statistics

- ★ @benjamini1995 — controlling the false discovery rate.
- @storey2003 — statistical significance for genome-wide studies (q-values).
- @efron2002 — empirical Bayes methods and FDR for microarrays.
- @lever2017 — principal component analysis (Points of Significance).
